text: French Revolution
testCases.query:
The French Revolution (1789–1799) began with a fiscal crisis that forced Louis XVI to convene the Estates-General for the first time since 1614. The Third Estate — representing roughly 98% of the population — broke away to form the National Assembly after being locked out of deliberations. The storming of the Bastille on 14 July 1789 became the revolution's symbolic starting point. The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen (August 1789) proclaimed liberty, equality, and popular sovereignty as founding principles.

The Revolution moved through distinct phases. A constitutional monarchy (1789–1792) produced the Constitution of 1791. The radical Jacobin phase brought the Reign of Terror (1793–1794) under Robespierre: approximately 17,000 people were formally executed and up to 40,000 died in custody. The Thermidorian Reaction (July 1794) ended the Terror with Robespierre's arrest and execution. The Directory (1795–1799) governed until Napoleon's coup of 18 Brumaire terminated the revolutionary period.

Root causes combined Enlightenment ideology, fiscal bankruptcy, food shortages, and structural inequality between the Three Estates: First (clergy), Second (nobility), and Third (everyone else). The Revolution's long-term legacy includes the spread of republican ideals, modern nationalism, and the Napoleonic Code across Europe.

testCases.label: text: black holes
testCases.query:
A black hole is a region of spacetime where gravity is so strong that nothing — not even light — can escape once past the event horizon. Stellar black holes form when massive stars (typically above 20 solar masses) exhaust their nuclear fuel, collapse under gravity in a supernova, and leave a singularity of theoretically infinite density. At the singularity, general relativity breaks down; a quantum theory of gravity would be needed to describe conditions there.

The event horizon is not a physical surface but a mathematical boundary — the radius at which escape velocity equals the speed of light. For a non-rotating black hole, this is the Schwarzschild radius: r = 2GM/c². Black holes are fully characterised by just three observable properties — mass, electric charge, and angular momentum — a result known as the no-hair theorem. Rotating black holes (Kerr black holes) drag surrounding spacetime in a process called frame dragging.

Hawking radiation, predicted theoretically in 1974, suggests black holes emit thermal radiation and slowly evaporate over astronomical timescales; it has never been observed directly. Supermassive black holes — millions to billions of solar masses — sit at the centres of most large galaxies. The one at the Milky Way's centre, Sagittarius A*, has a mass of about 4 million solar masses.
